passage:
In the quarterly review, Imran, her manager, read out Rehana's mistakes to the whole team, one by one, and grinned at his own joke about the last one. Rehana's face burned. She kept her eyes on her notebook until the meeting ended.

Back at her desk she opened a blank email. Her hands were unsteady and her breath was short, but the words came easily: I resign, effective immediately. She read it once and pressed send at seven that night, holding no other offer and only one month's rent saved.

It felt like fresh air for exactly one night. In the morning came the questions: how would she pay next month, and who would give her a reference? Two colleagues she liked stopped replying to her messages.

qa.q: What time did Rehana send the resignation email?
How was Rehana feeling when the words came so easily?
qa.a: Rehana was humiliated and angry, and the quick email was a way of escaping the shame.

qa.q: What could Rehana have done instead that evening, and why?
qa.a: Rehana could have waited a few days and spoken to a trusted person, because a decision made in the heat of humiliation is harder to undo.

qa.q: How might Imran see the sudden resignation?
qa.a: Imran may be surprised and uncomfortable, realising his public criticism contributed, and the team is left short-handed.

grounding: Humiliated in a review, the employee resigns by email that evening with no other offer, leaving an income gap and burned bridges.

"You resigned? Tonight?" Akash stared at his sister across the dining table.
"He tore my report apart in front of the whole team, Akash. Called it 'intern-level'. I've never been so humiliated." Tanuja's voice shook. "So I came home and wrote the email."
"What did it say?"
"That I quit, effective in two weeks, and that his feedback style is toxic. I copied the whole team."
"Do you have another offer?"
She was quiet. "No."
"Tanuja, the rent here is split two ways."
"I know. It felt so good pressing send. Like I could breathe."
Akash rubbed his face. "And now?"
She scrolled through her phone. "Priyanka from HR just messaged. She says she can't give me a reference after an email like that." Tanuja put the phone face down. "I thought I was freeing myself."

qa.q: Who did Tanuja copy on the resignation email?
How did Tanuja feel when she pressed send, and how does that shift?
qa.a: She felt free and able to breathe at first, but that turns into regret when HR says there will be no reference.

qa.q: What could Tanuja have done that evening instead of resigning?
qa.a: She could have written the email and left it unsent for a few days, then talked to HR or a mentor about the review, keeping her options and her references.

qa.q: How is Akash affected by Tanuja's decision?
qa.a: Akash is worried, because they split the rent two ways and Tanuja now has no other offer.

grounding: Shows an employee who, humiliated in a review, resigns the same evening with no offer, feeling free but losing income and burning bridges.

passage:
I still remember the Monday review. Jeevan, my manager, put my campaign numbers on the big screen and said, "This is what happens when you don't check your work." Twelve people looked at me.
I went home, ate nothing, and at eleven I sent my resignation. No new job. No talk with anyone. Just a three-line email saying I was leaving at the end of the month.
The next morning I felt amazing, honestly. Lighter.
That lasted about a week. Then came the searching. Two months with no offers. I moved back to my parents' flat. When a recruiter at another agency called Jeevan for a reference, I heard later that it was very brief.
Was the review unfair? Partly. But I let one evening decide the next six months.
Rajni, if you're reading this in your drafts folder next year: sleep on it first.

qa.q: How many people were in the room during Rajni's review?
qa.a: Twelve people looked at Rajni during the review.

qa.q: How did Rajni feel the morning after resigning?
qa.a: Rajni felt amazing and lighter, a sense of relief that lasted about a week before the search began.

qa.q: What approach would have suited Rajni better that night?
qa.a: Waiting at least until morning and talking to someone before deciding, and job hunting while still employed, would have avoided the long gap.

qa.q: How might Jeevan see Rajni's sudden resignation?
qa.a: Jeevan may have been surprised and a little defensive, which could explain why the reference was very brief.

grounding: Shows an employee resigning the same night as a humiliating review with no other offer, feeling free at first but losing income and goodwill.
